name: Cognitive Restructuring
description: Identifying an automatic negative thought, examining the evidence for and against it, and replacing it with a more balanced, realistic thought.
citation: Beck, A. T. (1979). Cognitive Therapy of Depression. Guilford Press.
limitations: Requires enough self-reflective capacity to separate a thought from a fact; not a substitute for treatment of clinical depression.

name: Decatastrophizing ("What If" Technique)
description: Walking through the actually-likely outcome, the worst-case outcome, and how one would cope with the worst case, to reduce the perceived unbearability of a feared event.
citation: Beck, A. T., Emery, G., & Greenberg, R. L. (1985). Anxiety Disorders and Phobias: A Cognitive Perspective. Basic Books.
limitations: Can feel invalidating if used before the person feels heard; should follow, not replace, emotional validation.

name: Behavioral Activation
description: Scheduling small, concrete, achievable activities (especially ones tied to values or past enjoyment) to counteract withdrawal and low mood, rather than waiting to 'feel like it' first.
citation: Jacobson, N. S., Dobson, K. S., Truax, P. A., et al. (1996). A component analysis of cognitive-behavioral treatment for depression. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 64(2), 295-304.
limitations: Effortful to start precisely when motivation is lowest; works best with very small first steps.

name: Self-Compassion Practice
description: Responding to one's own suffering or perceived failure with the same kindness, warmth, and understanding one would offer a good friend, rather than harsh self-judgment.
citation: Neff, K. D. (2003). Self-compassion: An alternative conceptualization of a healthy attitude toward oneself. Self and Identity, 2(2), 85-101.
limitations: Can initially feel unfamiliar or 'soft' to people used to self-criticism as a motivator; benefits usually build with repeated practice.

name: Values Clarification (ACT)
description: Distinguishing what genuinely matters to the person (their values) from the anxious thought itself, then identifying one small action in line with that value regardless of the discomfort.
citation: Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (1999). Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: An Experiential Approach to Behavior Change. Guilford Press.
limitations: Not aimed at eliminating the anxious thought, which can be unsatisfying for someone wanting the thought itself to go away.

name: Behavioral Experiment
description: Turning a feared prediction into a small, testable real-world experiment (e.g. 'if I ask, they will say no') to gather actual evidence instead of relying on assumption.
citation: Bennett-Levy, J., Butler, G., Fennell, M., et al. (2004). Oxford Guide to Behavioural Experiments in Cognitive Therapy. Oxford University Press.
limitations: Needs a genuinely testable, low-stakes prediction; not suitable for high-risk or irreversible situations.

name: Gratitude Practice
description: Deliberately noticing and recording a small number of specific positive things, which has been shown to shift attention away from a purely deficit-focused view of one's life.
citation: Emmons, R. A., & McCullough, M. E. (2003). Counting blessings versus burdens: An experimental investigation of gratitude and subjective well-being. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 84(2), 377-389.
limitations: Not appropriate as a first response to acute distress; can read as dismissive if offered too early.

name: Structured Problem-Solving
description: Breaking an overwhelming situation into a defined problem, a brainstormed list of options, a chosen option, and one concrete next action, to counter paralysis in the face of a large stressor.
citation: D'Zurilla, T. J., & Nezu, A. M. (2007). Problem-Solving Therapy: A Positive Approach to Clinical Intervention (3rd ed.). Springer.
limitations: Less useful when the core issue is an internal emotional state rather than an external, actionable problem.
